issues.legal_issue: A deceased appellant’s right of appeal does not survive to the remaining appellants under the rule for survivorship when they have not established that they and the deceased formed a joint Hindu family.
material_facts: Nine plaintiffs jointly filed a second appeal; one appellant died while it was pending, and no timely application was made to bring his legal representatives on the record.
Although the surviving appellants were given time to provide evidence that they formed a joint Hindu family with the deceased, their affidavits did not make that assertion.
The application to substitute the deceased appellant’s sons described them as his heirs and legal representatives.
issues.conclusion: The surviving appellants could not continue the appeal on the basis that the right to appeal survived to them alone; the appeal abated as against the deceased appellant.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXII, rules 2, 3 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, survivorship applies only where the right to sue or appeal survives to the remaining parties. The evidence did not establish that the appellants formed a joint Hindu family or that the deceased appellant’s right to appeal survived to them.

rule.if: joint_plaintiff_appeal and appellant_dies_during_appeal and no_timely_substitution and no_proof_of_joint_family

predicates.joint_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs jointly filed an appeal.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.no_timely_substitution: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not brought on the record within the required time.
predicates.no_proof_of_joint_family: The remaining appellants did not establish that they and the deceased appellant formed a joint family through which the right of appeal survived to them.

issues.definition: When plaintiffs jointly appeal, an appellant dies, substitution is not timely, and the survivors do not establish the relevant joint-family relationship, the survivors cannot continue by survivorship.

issues.legal_issue: The power to appeal against an entire decree on a ground common to multiple plaintiffs does not permit surviving appellants to continue an appeal jointly filed by all plaintiffs after one appellant’s appeal has abated.
material_facts: All nine plaintiffs jointly filed the second appeal while the deceased appellant was alive and was himself an appellant.
The decree concerned a common, joint right to obtain ejectment, and the appeal abated as against the deceased appellant when his legal representatives were not substituted in time.
The respondents’ position was that allowing the survivors to proceed could result in inconsistent decrees concerning the joint right.
issues.conclusion: Order XLI, rule 4 did not apply, and the appeal could not proceed in favour of the surviving appellants after the deceased appellant’s appeal had abated.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows one plaintiff or defendant to appeal from the whole decree where it proceeds on a ground common to all, but it did not apply because all plaintiffs had jointly filed this appeal and the survivors had not filed it as representatives of the deceased. Order XXII operates during the appeal and requires timely substitution; its abatement provisions are not overridden by rule 4. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram for the principle that abatement makes the decree final against the deceased party’s legal representatives and prevents direct or indirect modification affecting their rights. It approved Ramphal Sahu v. Babu Satdeo Jha, Amin Chand v. Baldeo Sahai Ganga Sahai, Baij Nath v. Ram Bharose, Nanak v. Ahmad Ali, Pyarelal v. Sikhar Chand, Raghu Sutar v. Narusingha Nath, Venkata Ram Rao v. Narayana, and Sonahar Ali v. Mukbul Ali, and disapproved the contrary approaches in Shripad Balwant v. Nagu Kusheba, Satulal Bhattachariya v. Asiruddin Shaikh, and Somasundaram Chettiar v. Vaithilinga Mudaliar.

rule.if: joint_plaintiff_appeal and all_plaintiffs_joined_in_filing and common_ground_for_all and joint_indivisible_right and appellant_dies_during_appeal and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased

predicates.joint_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs brought an appeal from a decree.
predicates.all_plaintiffs_joined_in_filing: All plaintiffs, including the later-deceased appellant, jointly filed the appeal while that appellant was alive.
predicates.common_ground_for_all: The decree under appeal rested on a ground common to all the plaintiffs.
predicates.joint_indivisible_right: The plaintiffs’ claimed right was joint and could not be divided without affecting the parties’ rights against one another.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal abated as against the deceased appellant because the required substitution was not made in time.

issues.definition: When all plaintiffs jointly appeal on a common ground concerning an indivisible joint right and one appellant’s appeal abates on that appellant’s death, the appeal cannot proceed for the survivors.

issues.legal_issue: The appellate court’s broad power to make further orders cannot be used to continue an appeal that is not competent after abatement or to defeat the finality of the decree as to the deceased appellant.
material_facts: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not substituted in time, so the decree became final against them.
The surviving appellants sought to rely on the appellate court’s broad powers even though the appeal could not competently proceed after the abatement.
The failure to take steps for substitution was attributable to the deceased appellant’s legal representatives and the surviving appellants.
issues.conclusion: Order XLI, rule 33 did not apply because the surviving appellants’ appeal was not competent in the circumstances; that rule could not be used to grant relief affecting the deceased appellant’s rights or nullify abatement.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the appellate court a wide discretion, including in exceptional cases where its non-exercise would make adjustment of parties’ rights difficult, but does not make an incompetent appeal competent or override abatement under Order XXII. The Court relied on Mahomed Khaleel Shirazi & Sons v. Los Panneries Lyonnaises, which held that rule 33 was not intended to apply to an appeal that was not competent against a party. The Court also explained that exercising the power to grant relief for the deceased appellant would create contradictory decrees and improperly defeat the finality resulting from abatement.

rule.if: plaintiff_appeal_after_decree and appellant_dies_during_appeal and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased and surviving_appeal_is_incompetent

predicates.plaintiff_appeal_after_decree: A plaintiff brought an appeal from a decree.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal abated as against the deceased appellant because the required substitution was not made in time.
predicates.surviving_appeal_is_incompetent: After the abatement, the surviving appellants’ appeal could not competently proceed in a way that affected the deceased appellant’s rights.

issues.definition: When an appellant dies, the appeal abates as to that appellant, and the survivors’ appeal is incompetent, the court’s broad appellate power cannot restore the abated appeal.
